paras: The lynching of Nathan Laird was the hanging of a Black prisoner by a mob of masked horsemen who took him from the county jail at Sardis, Mississippi, early on June 21, 1882. Laird, called Nathan Lucid in the wire reports, had been jailed to await trial on a charge of raping the daughter of a white widow. The Jackson wire carried the news across the country, while the Sardis weekly printed a detailed account of the mob forcing the jail keys from the sheriff's household.

According to the Panola Weekly Star, on the night of June 15-16 Laird entered the home of Mrs. Taylor, a widow living seven or eight miles east of Sardis, struck her with a pistol when she hit him with a board, and raped her daughter. The Memphis Public Ledger, calling him "Frank Layard," told a different story, in which he beat the widow insensible and was driven off before any rape by her thirteen-year-old daughter, who burned him with a firebrand. Laird was found asleep in a gully near town, arrested, and brought before 'Squire Balch, who committed him to jail to await trial on Wednesday, June 21. The Star conceded that "all the evidence against him was circumstantial," though it reported that he had admitted to "certain parties" striking Mrs. Taylor.

At about half past one in the morning, a company of masked horsemen numbering "about seventy-five, more or less" came to the jail and demanded the prisoner. Deputy Sheriff George V. Lester refused to give up the keys, and so did Sheriff Smith, who was sick in bed, until the mob's leader ordered the doors broken down and Mrs. Smith, fearing for her husband, handed the keys over. The men made Lester show them the cell, and Laird, crying "murder!", was rushed across the courthouse yard, put on a mule, and ridden with the company about one mile out East Lee street to a small oak tree.

The Star's surviving text breaks off at that point, but its headline says the body hung for eight hours. The Memphis Daily Appeal instead put the mob at 20 men and the tree half a mile south of town, and said the body hung for twenty-four hours. The Public Ledger placed the hanging about four miles east of Sardis.

The Star's headline announced a coroner's jury verdict, but the verdict itself is lost from the surviving text. The wire said the lynchers were unknown, and the Public Ledger reported that they were said to be strangers in Sardis, probably from the neighborhood of the alleged crime. No report of an arrest appears in the coverage. Laird's mother and other relatives refused to bury him, saying they "wanted dem dat hung him to bury him," and the county paid for his burial.

Most papers knew the event only from a Jackson dispatch of June 21, which named the victim Nathan Lucid and gave the charge as rape. Rewritten for news summaries, the charge became "indecent assault" in the Savannah Morning News, "felonious assault" in the Daily Gazette and the Lancaster Intelligencer, and "brutal assault" in the New-York Tribune, whose version had the mob entering the "Crown Court." Western papers such as the Cheyenne Daily Leader and the Salt Lake Herald datelined the item "Sardis, Wis." A week later, weekly crime roundups from Dakota to Michigan and Kansas were still reprinting a single line saying he had been lynched for an assault on a white woman.

The two Memphis papers covered the case as nearby news. The Public Ledger called him "a darky" and "the wretch" and praised the "gallant girl" who fought him off. The Panola Weekly Star condemned "the fiendish deed" but dwelt on the officers' refusal to give up the prisoner and admitted that no trial had tested the evidence.

The papers gave the victim three names: Nathan Laird in the Sardis paper and the Bismarck Tribune, Nathan Lucid in the wire, and Frank Layard in the Public Ledger. The Sardis paper, which knew his family, is the closest source. The Appeal's date, "the night of the 10 instant," conflicts with every other report of the night of June 20-21 and is probably a misprint.

reader.title: Lynching of Nathan Laird
bases: A mob took a Black prisoner charged with rape from the Sardis jail and hanged him (A3, A4, A13).

About seventy-five masked men (twenty in the Memphis Appeal) forced the jail keys from the sheriff's household, took out a prisoner awaiting trial on a rape charge and hanged him (A13, A6, A3); every report calls it a lynching by a mob (A2, A4, A15).
The Jackson wire (A3, A4), two Memphis papers (A6, A7) and the Sardis weekly (A13) independently report the taking from jail and the hanging.

accounts.label: Jackson wire
accounts.gist: An armed mob forcibly entered the county jail at Sardis early on June 21, took Nathan Lucid, colored, charged with rape or assault, and hanged him; the lynchers were unknown.

accounts.label: Panola Weekly Star (Sardis)
accounts.gist: About seventy-five masked horsemen came at 1:30 a.m., overrode the refusals of the sheriff and his deputy, got the keys from the sheriff's wife, and rode Nathan Laird about a mile out East Lee street to an oak tree; the paper says the evidence against him was circumstantial.

accounts.label: Memphis Public Ledger
accounts.gist: 'Frank Layard' was hanged about four miles east of Sardis after he had beaten the widow Taylor and been driven off by her daughter with a firebrand; the lynchers were said to be strangers.

accounts.label: Memphis Daily Appeal
accounts.gist: A mob of 20 took a Black prisoner jailed for the rape of a white lady and hanged him half a mile south of town, leaving the body for twenty-four hours.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Jackson wire as a one-line item in news summaries or crime columns, under heads such as 'Lynched' and 'A Negro Lynched in Mississippi'.
The Sardis weekly called the alleged rape 'the fiendish deed' yet stressed that the evidence was circumstantial and that the sheriff and deputy tried to save the prisoner.
The Memphis Public Ledger called him 'a darky' and 'the wretch', presented the assault as fact, and praised the 'gallant girl'.

record_check.dossier: One victim under three names: Nathan Laird (local paper), Nathan Lucid (wire), Frank Layard (Memphis Public Ledger)
Charged with rape of a white widow's daughter (local paper); wires vary between rape, indecent, felonious and brutal assault
About seventy-five masked horsemen, unidentified; said to be from the neighborhood of the alleged crime
The 10th comes only from the Memphis Appeal's garbled 'night of the 10 instant'; the lynching was early June 21

info: Early morning of Wednesday, June 21, 1882, about 1:30 a.m. (Tuesday night)
Taken from the county jail at Sardis, Miss.; hanged on a small oak tree about one mile out East Lee street (Panola Star); half a mile south of town (Appeal); four miles east of Sardis (Public Ledger)
One Black man, named Nathan Laird (Panola Star, Bismarck Tribune), Nathan Lucid (Jackson wire), or Frank Layard (Memphis Public Ledger)

Accused of raping the daughter of Mrs. Taylor, a widow living seven or eight miles east of Sardis, on the night of June 15-16 (Panola Star); of a murderous assault and attempted rape on the widow Taylor (Public Ledger); wires say rape, indecent, felonious or brutal assault
Masked horsemen; lynchers 'unknown' (wire); 'said to be strangers' in Sardis, probably from the neighborhood of the alleged crime (Public Ledger)
